chapter.name: Work, Energy, and Simple Machines
chapter.blurb: Defines work done by a constant force and its sign, introduces the work-energy theorem and the forms energy can take, develops kinetic energy and gravitational potential energy with the conservation of mechanical energy, defines power as the rate of doing work, and explains mechanical advantage for the pulley, inclined plane and lever.

scope_in.item: Define work done by a constant force as W = F x s (force applied x displacement in the direction of the force), with SI unit joule
Identify when work done on an object is zero: when the force is zero, when there is no displacement, or when the force acts perpendicular to the displacement
Determine the sign of work done: positive when force and displacement are in the same direction, negative when they are opposite
Solve numerical problems calculating work done, including negative work, given force and displacement (Examples 7.1, 7.2)
State the work-energy theorem: work done on an object (or a system of objects) equals the change in its energy, and that it holds even for non-constant forces
Identify different forms of energy (mechanical, thermal, light, sound, chemical, electrical, nuclear) and everyday examples of one form changing into another
Define kinetic energy as the energy an object has due to its motion, and derive/apply K = 1/2 m v^2 using the work-energy theorem
Solve numerical problems calculating kinetic energy, or the speed/mass from a given kinetic energy (Examples 7.4-7.6)
Define potential energy as energy stored due to deformation or the relative position of objects in a system (springs, magnets, charges, Earth-ball system), treated qualitatively
Derive and apply the formula for gravitational potential energy near the Earth's surface, U = mgh (Example 7.7)
Define mechanical energy as the sum of kinetic and potential energy, and state the law of conservation of mechanical energy for an object acted on only by gravity
Apply conservation of mechanical energy to solve problems involving falling objects, slides, pendulums and escape ramps (Examples 7.8-7.9)
Define power as the rate of doing work, P = W / t, with SI unit watt
Solve numerical problems calculating power, work done or time taken (Examples 7.10-7.11)
Define simple machines, effort, load and mechanical advantage = load / effort
Explain how a fixed pulley changes only the direction of the effort (mechanical advantage 1) and how a movable pulley / pulley system gives mechanical advantage greater than 1
Derive and apply the mechanical advantage of an inclined plane, MA = L / h (Example 7.12)
Identify the parts of a lever (fulcrum, load, effort, load arm, effort arm) and apply the balancing condition effort x effort arm = load x load arm, and MA = effort arm / load arm (Example 7.13)
Classify levers into Class I, II and III based on the relative positions of fulcrum, load and effort, with everyday examples of each
State that simple machines do not create energy or reduce total work done; they only change the magnitude or direction of the force needed

concepts.name: Work done by a constant force
concepts.description: Work done by a constant force as the product of force and displacement in the direction of the force, when work done is zero, and when it is positive or negative.
concepts.idea: Work is done on an object only when a force displaces it; work equals force times displacement along the force's direction.
concepts.rule: Work done W = F x s, where F is the constant force and s is the displacement of the object in the direction of F. Work is zero if F = 0, if s = 0, or if the force acts perpendicular to the displacement. Work is positive when force and displacement are in the same direction, and negative when they are in opposite directions. The SI unit of work is the joule (J), where 1 J = 1 N x 1 m.
concepts.example: A person applies a horizontal force of 50 N to push a box through a displacement of 4 m in the direction of the force. The work done is W = 50 N x 4 m = 200 J.

questions.q: A boy applies a horizontal force of 20 N to pull a toy cart through a distance of 5 m in the direction of the force. Calculate the work done by the boy on the cart.
s: Formula W = F x s

questions.q: A crate is pushed with a constant force of 150 N and moves 3 m in the direction of the force. Find the work done on the crate.
s: Formula W = F x s

questions.q: A father pushes his child's swing forward with a force of 25 N over a displacement of 2 m in the direction of the push, and then applies a backward force of 15 N over the next 1 m as the swing continues to move forward, in order to slow it down. Calculate the total work done by the father.
s: Work while pushing forward = 25 N x 2 m = 50 J
Work while slowing (force opposite to displacement) = -15 N x 1 m = -15 J
Total work = 50 J + (-15 J) = 35 J

questions.q: A crane exerts a constant upward force of 4000 N on a steel beam and raises it through a height of 12 m. Calculate the work done by the crane on the beam, and state whether this work is positive or negative.
s: Formula W = F x s
Value: 4000 N x 12 m = 48000 J
Sign: positive, since the force and displacement are both upward (same direction)

questions.q: A block is pulled along a rough floor by a horizontal force of 40 N through a distance of 5 m, while friction exerts a force of 40 N opposing the motion of the block. Calculate the work done on the block by (i) the applied force, and (ii) friction.
questions.a: 200 J by the applied force; -200 J by friction
s: Work done by the applied force = 40 N x 5 m = 200 J
Work done by friction = -40 N x 5 m = -200 J
Correct reasoning that friction acts opposite to the displacement, giving negative work

questions.q: A weightlifter raises a barbell of weight 500 N vertically through 2 m and then slowly lowers it back to the starting point through the same 2 m, always applying a force equal to the weight of the barbell. Calculate the work done by the weightlifter (i) while raising the barbell, (ii) while lowering it, and (iii) the total work done over the complete raise-and-lower cycle. Explain your answer to (iii) in terms of the direction of the force and the displacement.
questions.a: +1000 J while raising, -1000 J while lowering, total 0 J
s: Work while raising = 500 N x 2 m = +1000 J
Work while lowering = -500 N x 2 m = -1000 J (force still upward, but displacement is now downward)
Total work over the cycle = 1000 J + (-1000 J) = 0 J
Explanation: in lowering, the applied force is upward while the displacement is downward, so the two works are opposite in sign and cancel

questions.q: Consider the following statements about work done by a force: (I) Work done can be zero even when both the force and the displacement are non-zero. (II) Work done is always positive whenever a force acts on a moving object. Which is or are correct?
A crate is pushed 4 m by a force of 50 N in the direction of the push, while friction of 20 N opposes the motion over the same 4 m. What is the net work done on the crate by both forces combined?

A porter carries a suitcase horizontally at a constant height while walking forward, and later climbs a flight of stairs carrying the same suitcase to a floor above. In which of these two actions does the porter do work on the suitcase against gravity, and in which does he do zero work against gravity? Justify your answer using the direction of the force and the displacement in each case.
questions.a: Zero work while walking horizontally; positive work while climbing the stairs
s: Walking horizontally: zero work against gravity, since the upward supporting force is perpendicular to the horizontal displacement
Climbing stairs: positive work against gravity, since there is a vertical component of displacement in the direction of the upward force

questions.q: A student says, 'Since I feel tired after pushing hard against a locked door that does not move, I must have done a lot of work on the door.' Evaluate this statement using the scientific definition of work, and explain why the student feels tired even though no work is done on the door.
questions.a: The statement is scientifically incorrect: work done on the door is zero since it does not move; tiredness comes from internal muscular energy use, not work done on the door.
s: Evaluation: the statement is scientifically incorrect; work done on the door is zero because it does not move (s = 0)
Explanation: the student feels tired because muscles repeatedly contract and use internal (chemical) energy even without moving the door
Conclusion distinguishing the everyday sense of 'work' from the scientific definition

questions.a: Any valid original scenario where the applied force is opposite to the displacement, giving W = -30 N x 2 m = -60 J.
s: Original situation described with the force opposite to the displacement

concepts.name: Work-energy theorem and forms of energy
concepts.description: The work-energy theorem relating work done on an object to the change in its energy, and the different forms energy can take and change into.
concepts.idea: Doing work on an object changes its energy; energy exists in many forms and can be transformed from one form to another.
concepts.rule: The work-energy theorem states that work done on an object (or a system of objects) equals the change in its energy; this holds even when the forces involved are not constant. The SI unit of energy is the same as that of work, the joule (J). Energy can appear in different forms -- mechanical (due to motion or position), thermal, light, sound, chemical, electrical and nuclear -- and it can be transferred or transformed from one form to another, e.g. electrical energy to light energy in a bulb, or chemical energy in food to mechanical energy in muscles.
concepts.example: A fielder does positive work on a cricket ball by throwing it, and the ball gains kinetic energy equal to the work done on it, illustrating the work-energy theorem.

questions.q: A pot is raised to a height by doing 40 J of work against gravity. According to the work-energy theorem, how much potential energy does the pot gain? Name the form of energy involved.

questions.q: A toy car's spring-driven motor does 5 J of work on the car, giving it 5 J of kinetic energy. As the car moves, friction does -5 J of work on it. Using the work-energy theorem, find the car's final kinetic energy, and explain what happens to the car's motion.

s: Falling: the toy's gravitational potential energy converts into kinetic energy
Landing: kinetic energy is used to do work deforming the mat, ending up mostly as thermal energy, consistent with the 40 J of work done

Catch: the goalkeeper's hands do negative work, removing the ball's kinetic energy to stop it

concepts.name: Kinetic energy
concepts.description: Kinetic energy as the energy possessed by an object due to its motion, derived from the work-energy theorem, and its formula K = 1/2 m v^2.
concepts.idea: A moving object can do work because of its motion; this capacity is called kinetic energy and depends on both the object's mass and the square of its speed.
concepts.rule: The kinetic energy of an object of mass m moving with velocity v is K = 1/2 m v^2. An object at rest has zero kinetic energy. Kinetic energy has no direction (it is a scalar) and is measured in joules. Doubling the mass doubles the kinetic energy at the same speed; doubling the speed quadruples the kinetic energy at the same mass, because v is squared.
concepts.example: A 0.2 kg cricket ball moving at 40 m/s has kinetic energy K = 0.5 x 0.2 x 40 squared = 160 J.

questions.q: A car of mass 1200 kg travelling at 15 m/s brakes and comes to rest after travelling 20 m under a constant braking force. Using the work-energy theorem and the formula for kinetic energy, find (i) the initial kinetic energy of the car, and (ii) the magnitude of the constant braking force.
s: Initial kinetic energy = 1/2 x 1200 x 15 squared = 135000 J

Force = work done / displacement = 135000 / 20
Force = 6750 N

questions.q: Consider the following statements about kinetic energy: (I) If the speed of an object is tripled, its kinetic energy becomes three times as much. (II) If the mass of an object is tripled at the same speed, its kinetic energy becomes three times as much. Which is or are correct?

questions.q: A student claims that 'if I want to double an object's kinetic energy, I should double its speed.' Evaluate whether this method actually doubles the kinetic energy, showing your reasoning with the formula for kinetic energy.
questions.a: The claim is incorrect: doubling the speed makes the kinetic energy 4 times as much, not 2 times; the speed should be multiplied by the square root of 2 to exactly double the kinetic energy.
s: Evaluation: the claim is incorrect
Reasoning: doubling the speed makes K proportional to (2v) squared = 4v squared, i.e. 4 times, not 2 times, the original kinetic energy
Correct method: the speed should be multiplied by the square root of 2 to exactly double the kinetic energy

concepts.name: Potential energy and conservation of mechanical energy
concepts.description: Gravitational potential energy as energy stored due to an object's height above the ground, and the law of conservation of mechanical energy for an object moving under gravity alone.
concepts.idea: An object raised above the ground has the capacity to do work because of its position; as it falls, this stored potential energy converts into kinetic energy while the total mechanical energy stays the same.
concepts.rule: The gravitational potential energy of an object of mass m at height h above a chosen reference level is U = mgh. Mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic energy and potential energy. When only gravity acts on an object (no friction or air resistance), its mechanical energy is conserved: as it falls, potential energy decreases exactly as much as kinetic energy increases, so KE + PE stays constant at every point of the motion.
concepts.example: A ball of mass 1 kg held at a height of 5 m has potential energy U = 1 x 10 x 5 = 50 J (taking g = 10 m/s squared); as it falls freely to the ground, this 50 J converts entirely into kinetic energy just before it lands.

questions.q: A skateboarder of mass 50 kg starts from rest at the top of a ramp 5 m high and rolls down to the bottom, where the ramp curves back up to a second, lower hill of height 2 m. Assuming no friction, use conservation of mechanical energy to find (i) the skateboarder's speed at the bottom of the first ramp, and (ii) the speed at the top of the 2 m hill. concepts.name: Power
concepts.description: Power as the rate at which work is done, its formula and SI unit, and calculating power in everyday and mechanical situations.
concepts.idea: Doing the same amount of work faster requires more power; power measures how quickly work is done or energy is transferred.
concepts.rule: Power is defined as the rate at which work is done: P = W / t, where W is the work done and t is the time taken. The SI unit of power is the watt (W), where 1 W = 1 joule of work done per second (1 W = 1 J/s). Doing more work in the same time, or the same work in less time, both require greater power.
concepts.example: A weightlifter who lifts a 75 kg mass by 2 m in 5 seconds does 1500 J of work, so her power is 1500 J divided by 5 s, which equals 300 W.

concepts.name: Simple machines: pulley, inclined plane and lever
concepts.description: Simple machines that make tasks easier by changing the magnitude or direction of an applied force, including the pulley, the inclined plane and the lever, and their mechanical advantage.
concepts.idea: A simple machine does not reduce the total work needed for a task, but it lets us trade off the force required against the distance over which it is applied, or change the direction of the force.
concepts.rule: Mechanical advantage = load / effort. A fixed pulley changes only the direction of the effort and has mechanical advantage 1; a movable pulley (or pulley system) can give mechanical advantage greater than 1. For an inclined plane of length L raising a load to height h, mechanical advantage = L / h. For a lever, the load arm and effort arm satisfy effort x effort arm = load x load arm, so mechanical advantage = effort arm / load arm. Levers are classified as Class I (fulcrum between load and effort, e.g. seesaw, scissors), Class II (load between fulcrum and effort, e.g. wheelbarrow, bottle opener) and Class III (effort between fulcrum and load, e.g. tweezers, broom). Machines do not create energy; the work put in equals the useful work got out, ignoring friction.
concepts.example: A ramp of length 5 m used to raise a load to a height of 1 m has a mechanical advantage of L/h = 5/1 = 5, meaning the effort required is one-fifth of the load's weight.
